title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
The question
Every number the American Community Survey publishes is an estimate drawn from a sample, not a count. That means every number comes with a margin of error — a statement about how wrong it might be.
In this analysis, I’m looking to see how population and the measurement of reliability are related, using the number of college-educated individuals in each county as an example.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
Pulling the data

my_state <- "CA"        # two-letter abbreviation of state
my_variable <- "B15003_022"     # variable code


county_data <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = my_variable,
  state = my_state,
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5"
)

A margin of error of 3,000 means something very different for an estimate of 20,000 than for an estimate of 200,000. To compare across places, we need it as a percentage.

county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = moe / estimate * 100)


county_data %>%
  arrange(desc(moe_pct)) %>%
  select(NAME, estimate, moe, moe_pct) %>%
  head(10)

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
section: Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
text:
Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
To answer this we need population and our variable side by side, in the same row. That means a wide pull.

county_wide <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = c(myvar = my_variable,
                pop   = "B01003_001"),
  state = my_state,
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)

head(county_wide)

# A tibble: 6 × 6
  GEOID NAME                         myvarE myvarM    popE  popM
  <chr> <chr>                         <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl> <dbl>
1 06001 Alameda County, California   341463   4001 1651949    NA
2 06003 Alpine County, California       264    102    1695   234
3 06005 Amador County, California      5027    492   41029    NA
4 06007 Butte County, California      28185   1349  209470    NA
5 06009 Calaveras County, California   5242    616   45995    NA
6 06011 Colusa County, California      1579    339   21895    NA


In this table, popE = estimate, and popM = MOE.

county_wide <- county_wide %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = myvarM / myvarE * 100) %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 5  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 15 ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  ))

The following block compares the average population of counties in each reliability category.

county_wide %>%
  group_by(reliability) %>%
  summarize(
    n_counties = n(),
    avg_population = mean(popE)
  )

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  reliability     n_counties avg_population
  <chr>                <int>          <dbl>
1 High confidence         28       1310938.
2 Low confidence          10         15660.
3 Moderate                20        118996.


We can see here that population is clearly correlated with confidence in deriving the population statistics; high-confidence counties have by far the highest population, and low-confidence counties have by far the lowest population numbers.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
What this means for policy
Sierra County, located in a rural area in Northern California, has the state’s second-lowest population and scored the lowest in our reliability estimate. The neighboring Alpine County, which has the lowest population in the state, only scored slightly higher. Conversely, Los Angeles County, which has the highest population in the state, had the highest score for reliability.
This trend is related to how the ACS collects data; since it is based on a sample percentage rather than a complete survey of every person in the county, smaller counties have less people included in the study. With a smaller sample size, chances are higher that there may be variations in the study that aren’t necessarily representative of the whole. On the other hand, larger counties have larger samples that lead to more reliable estimates, as any variation is generally smoothed out the large number of observations.
For our variable (people with college educations), this could have the potential impact of improper funding allocation to areas that already have enough, as well as the diversion of education funds that could be sorely needed in a smaller county. For example, if it is improperly estimated that very people in Alpine County are college-educated (which is highly correlated with their children not going to college), while many people actually do want to go to college, the county could be passed over when it’s time to build a new university (like a CSU).

Coefficient of Variation (CV)
This is a relative measure of sampling error.
Low CV -> 15%; high reliability
Medium CV-> 15-30%; medium reliability
High CV -> 30+%; high sampling error, low reliability
moe_sum() -> adding estimates together
moe_prop -> one estimate as share of another
moe_ratio() -> poverty_num / household_income






Tip



90% of the time in a normal distribution, the value will fall within 1.645 standard deviations of the mean.




ACS MOE

Tells us the 90% confidence interval; a higher value is worse
Estimate could be 20% +- 3.0 standard deviations

text:
GIS with R

Coordinate Reference Systems (CRS)

2 main families of CRS: geographic and projected

Geographic Coordinate System (datum): units are in degrees from center of Earth

Ellipsoid used to approximate the geoid; many different kinds of ellipsoids with different flattening ratios
NAD27 -> first datum/geographic coordinate system
WGS84 is GPS standard
Line of latitude is at equator; line of longitude is at the Prime Meridian
Lat is flat

Projected Coordinate System: need to flatten geoid into a 2D surface

Conic, cylindrical, and planar coordinate systems
Projections can either preserve shapes, areas, distance, or direction

Make sure you’re checking if your state plane is in feet or meters
If state plane isn’t convenient (for long/large states), use UTM zones



All spatial data comes with a coordinate reference system; it comes with a geometry column that has coordinates






Tip



st_set_crs() -> 2272 # adds the correct CRS label, but doesn’t change actual coordinates

title: Assignment 3: Verify the Claim
text:
This analysis attempts to measure the accuracy of a 2018 article by the Philadelphia Media Network, “New Census figures on Philly neighborhoods show inequality, high numbers of whites living in poverty”. This article uses American Community Survey (ACS) data to conduct a neighborhood-by-neighborhood analysis of poverty and demographic conditions across Philadelphia.
According to the article, conditions in Philadelphia have gotten increasingly worse over the last 2 decades, with the following examples as proof:
The purpose of this analysis is to verify some of the claims made in the article by reconstructing the analysis of the ACS data and testing if the reported changes in the article are statistically significant.

title: Assignment 3: Verify the Claim
text:
Part 1: Import Data & Create Tables
First, we install all required packages. An API key from the US Census Bureau is required for this project, and it needs to be installed before any data can be fetched. A key can be easily obtained here.


Show code
# Install required packages

library(tidycensus)
library(tidyverse)


After installing all the packages and confirming the API key is set up, we can start importing data from the ACS table.
For this analysis, we will use the following codes:

B17001_001: total population of an area for which poverty can be determined.
B17001_002: total number of people in that area who fall below the poverty line.



Show code
# Variables from ACS table: total in poverty and total below
poverty_vars <- c(
  total_poverty = "B17001_001",

title: Assignment 3: Verify the Claim
text:
Part 2: Testing
In this portion of our analysis, we want to determine how reliable our data for each census tract is. First, we calculate the MOE of the poverty rate for each census.


Show code
# Calculate poverty rate and its MOE

# 2006-2010
poverty_2006_2010 <- poverty_2006_2010 %>%
  mutate(
    poverty_rate = below_povertyE / total_povertyE,
    
    poverty_rate_moe = moe_prop(
      num = below_povertyE,
      denom = total_povertyE,
      moe_num = below_povertyM,
      moe_denom = total_povertyM
    )
  )

# 2013-2017
poverty_2013_2017 <- poverty_2013_2017 %>%
  mutate(
    poverty_rate = below_povertyE / total_povertyE,
    
    poverty_rate_moe = moe_prop(
      num = below_povertyE,
      denom = total_povertyE,
      moe_num = below_povertyM,
      moe_denom = total_povertyM
    )
  )


We also want to calculate the coefficient of variation. We can do this using the two formulas below:
\[ SE = \frac{\text{MOE}}{1.645} \] And: \[ CV = \frac{\text{SE}}{estimate} * 100 \]
We use the thresholds determined by Jurjevich et al. (2018) for this analysis:

CV < 12% is reliable
CV > 12% and CV < 40% is somewhat reliable
CV > 40% is unreliable



Show code
# CV Calculations

poverty_2006_2010 <- poverty_2006_2010 %>%
  mutate(
    poverty_rate_se = poverty_rate_moe / 1.645,
    poverty_rate_cv = (poverty_rate_se / poverty_rate) * 100,
    
    reliability = case_when(
      poverty_rate_cv < 12 ~ "Reliable",
      poverty_rate_cv <= 40 ~ "Somewhat reliable",
      poverty_rate_cv > 40 ~ "Unreliable",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    )
  )

poverty_2013_2017 <- poverty_2013_2017 %>%
  mutate(
    poverty_rate_se = poverty_rate_moe / 1.645,
    poverty_rate_cv = (poverty_rate_se / poverty_rate) * 100,
    
    reliability = case_when(
      poverty_rate_cv < 12 ~ "Reliable",
      poverty_rate_cv <= 40 ~ "Somewhat reliable",
      poverty_rate_cv > 40 ~ "Unreliable",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    )
  )


After these calculations, we join the two periods together to create one dataset with one row per tract using an inner join.






Tip



We use an inner join because we want tracts that have data in both periods for the change calculation.




Show code
poverty_change <- poverty_2006_2010 %>%
  select(
    GEOID,
    NAME,
    poverty_rate_2006_2010 = poverty_rate,
    poverty_moe_2006_2010 = poverty_rate_moe,
    poverty_cv_2006_2010 = poverty_rate_cv,
    reliability_2006_2010 = reliability
  ) %>%
  inner_join(
    poverty_2013_2017 %>%
      select(
        GEOID,
        poverty_rate_2013_2017 = poverty_rate,
        poverty_moe_2013_2017 = poverty_rate_moe,
        poverty_cv_2013_2017 = poverty_rate_cv,
        reliability_2013_2017 = reliability
      ),
    by = "GEOID"
  )


Finally, we calculate the change in poverty rates by simply subtracting the 2006-10 rate from the newer 2013-17 rate.


Show code
poverty_change <- poverty_change %>%
  mutate(
    change = poverty_rate_2013_2017 - poverty_rate_2006_2010
  )

# To make it easier to read, convert proportions into percents

poverty_change <- poverty_change %>%
  mutate(
    change_percentage_points = change * 100
  )


To calculate the MOE of the change between the two periods, we can use this formula:
\[\text{MOE}_{\text{change}} = \sqrt{\text{MOE}_1^2 + \text{MOE}_2^2}\]


Show code
poverty_change <- poverty_change %>% mutate(
  change_moe = sqrt( poverty_moe_2006_2010^2 + poverty_moe_2013_2017^2 ) )




Show code
poverty_change <- poverty_change %>%
  mutate(
    change_lower = change - change_moe,
    change_upper = change + change_moe
  )


Now, we can check if the change is statistically significant at the 90% confidence interval. If the change is larger than the MOE we calculated earlier, the it is considered to be statistically significant.


Show code
poverty_change <- poverty_change %>%
  mutate(
    change_significant = abs(change) > change_moe
  )


Several census tracts have missing or incomplete values. We can run the script below to identify all of these tracts before deciding what to do with them.


Show code
poverty_change %>%
  filter(
    is.na(poverty_rate_2006_2010) |
      is.na(poverty_rate_2013_2017) |
      is.na(change)
  ) %>%
  select(
    GEOID,
    NAME,
    poverty_rate_2006_2010,
    poverty_rate_2013_2017,
    change
  )

Part 3: Results and Visualizations

Map
We haven’t imported the geometry of the tracts yet, so we need to run the following code block:

Finally, we display the map.


Show code

mutate(
  change_percentage_points = change * 100
) %>%
  ggplot() +
  geom_sf(
    aes(fill = change_percentage_points),
    color = "black"
  ) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    name = "Change in poverty rate\n(percentage points)"
  ) +
  theme_void() +
  labs(
    title = "Change in Poverty Rates Across Philadelphia",
    subtitle = "Census tract ACS 5-year estimates, 2006–2010 vs. 2013–2017",
    caption = "Grey values indicate no data."
  )









This map displays where there is a statistically significant change in poverty levels between the two censuses.


Show code
poverty_map %>%
  mutate(
    change_status = case_when(
      change_significant & change > 0 ~ "Detectable increase",
      change_significant & change < 0 ~ "Detectable decrease",
      TRUE ~ "No detectable change"
    )
  ) %>%
  ggplot() +
  geom_sf(
    aes(fill = change_status),
    color = "black",
    linewidth = 0.3
  ) +
  theme_void() +
  labs(
    title = "Statistically Significant Changes in Philadelphia Poverty Rates",
    subtitle = "Census tract ACS 5-year estimates, 2006–2010 vs. 2013–2017",
    fill = "Change status",
    caption = "A detectable change falls outside of the 90% confidence interval."
  )











Errorbar Visualization
This visualization shows only the statistically significant changes in poverty rates between the two time periods. The bars represent the estimated change, while the error bars (thinner black bars) represent the 90% margin of error.


Show code
poverty_analysis %>%
  filter(change_significant) %>%
  arrange(change) %>%
  slice_head(n = 15) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(GEOID, change), y = change * 100)) +
  geom_col(aes(fill = change > 0)) +
  geom_errorbar(
    aes(
      ymin = (change - change_moe) * 100,
      ymax = (change + change_moe) * 100
    ),
    width = 0.3
  ) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  coord_flip() +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Statistically Significant Changes in Poverty Rates",
    subtitle = "Philadelphia census tracts, 2006–2010 vs. 2013–2017",
    x = "Census tract",
    y = "Change in poverty rate (percentage points)",
    caption = "Bars show estimated change; error bars show the 90% margin of error."
  )











Reliability Table
This table displays the reliability of census tract poverty estimates based on their CV. Lower CV values indicate more reliable estimates.


Reliability table

  mutate(
    cv = pmax(
      poverty_cv_2006_2010,
      poverty_cv_2013_2017,

      cv < 12 ~ "🟢",
      cv <= 40 ~ "🟡",
      TRUE ~ "🔴"
    ),
    flag = case_when(
      cv < 12 ~ "Reliable",
      cv <= 40 ~ "Somewhat reliable",
      TRUE ~ "Unreliable"
    )
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(cv)) %>%
  select(
    dot,
    GEOID,
    poverty_cv_2006_2010,
    poverty_cv_2013_2017,
    flag

title: Assignment 3: Verify the Claim
text:
Part 4: Adjudication of Claims
A challenge of this project is that the census tracts found in the ACS dataset do not correspond to traditional boundaries of Philadelphia neighborhoods, which are somewhat informal and not collected or defined by the city for official use. Therefore, we have to estimate which tracts fall into the neighborhoods the article is analyzing. This process is naturally a source of error in this project.



Philadelphia Neighborhood Maps - Revolve Philly Group | Map …


The article particularly analyzes:

Fairhill (26): located in North Philadelphia; a predominantly white neighborhood. This registered the highest poverty rate in the city, 61 percent. This article explains how low-income neighborhoods are at particular risk of falling further into poverty, using Fairhill as an example.

Analysis: While the area around Fairhill did indeed see an average increase in poverty based on the map, few of these changes were statistically significant. Although the data does show that poverty increased slightly here, there is limited statistical evidence that poverty increased beyond the bounds of the variability of the ACS data.

Eastwick (10): located Southwest Philadelphia: a predominantly black and low-income neighborhood. This neighborhood showed the greatest poverty-rate increase of any community, going from 12 to 26 percent.

Analysis: From our map in part 3, there did not appear to be any statistically significant increases in poverty rate during the study period. In fact, some of the areas showed a statistically significant decrease in poverty rate. This contrasts with the claim of the article that the poverty rate has more than doubled in this area. Since all of our census tract data from Southwest Philadelphia shows either statistically significant decline in poverty or no statistically significant change, we can confidently refute this claim.

Holmesburg (50): located in Northeast Philadelphia: a predominantly white, working-class neighborhood. The article claims that poverty skyrocketed here, increasing more than 9x from 2 percent to 19 percent.

In the Northeast Philadelphia area, there is a mix of statistically significant increases in poverty, statistically significant decreases, and non-significant changes. It seems unlikely for a 9x increase in poverty to occur in an area around here, but since the neighborhood boundaries do not correspond exactly with the census tracts, we cannot confidently confirm or refute the claim specifically for Holmesburg.

Tioga-Nicetown (31): a predominantly black neighborhood located in Northwest Philadelphia: according to the article, the median income of this neighborhood dropped from 28,026 to 17,493, the largest drop in the city.

Analysis: in the census tract nearest to Tioga-Nicetown, a statistically significant increase in poverty can be observed. This corresponds with the 40 percent decrease in median income reported in the article. Areas bordering the neighborhood did not see statistically significant increases in poverty, however. The analysis in the article appears to be valid.

title: Assignment 3: Verify the Claim
text:
Part 5: Conclusion
Philadelphia continues to suffer from high poverty rates, particularly around minority-heavy areas in North Philly and West Philly. Income inequality is particularly high here, with statistically significant increases in wealth being observed between the 2010 and 2017 census. However, many lower-income areas in North Philly are seeing statistically significant decreases in poverty rates, which may suggest a sign of hope for these communities.
Therefore, this analysis provides mixed evidence for the article’s claims. Changes in poverty were not uniform across Philadelphia, and some areas in close proximity to each other experienced significant increases in poverty while some experienced significant decreases. Many other areas experienced no statistically significant changes at all. The data in many of these census tracts was deemed either “somewhat reliable” or “unreliable” based on its MOE, and a more detailed and complete survey of this area is necessary to get fully accurate results. Additionally, it would improve the accuracy of this analysis to conduct the survey by neighborhood instead of by census tract; however, it would be quite logistically challenging.

Every station gets its tract’s attributes:

Part 4: How far is the nearest station?
st_distance() returns a matrix, not a column. Look at its shape first:

centroids <- st_centroid(st_geometry(philly_tracts))

dim(st_distance(centroids, stations))

[1] 391 319


Instead, find the nearest station for each tract, then measure only that one distance:

nearest_idx <- st_nearest_feature(centroids, stations)

philly_tracts <- philly_tracts %>%
  mutate(
    dist_ft = as.numeric(
      st_distance(centroids, stations[nearest_idx, ], by_element = TRUE)
    ),
    dist_mi = dist_ft / 5280

section: Part 5: Buffers, filters, and cutting the dough
text:
Part 5: Buffers, filters, and cutting the dough
Build a half-mile zone around every station and merge the circles into one shape. Remember your units.

station_zone <- stations %>%
  st_buffer(dist = 0.5) %>%
  st_union()

Pick whole cookies: which tracts don’t touch the zone at all?

outside_zone <- philly_tracts %>%
  st_filter(station_zone, .predicate = st_disjoint)

nrow(outside_zone)

[1] 238


Cut the dough: what share of each tract’s area falls inside the zone?

philly_tracts <- philly_tracts %>%
  mutate(tract_area = as.numeric(st_area(.)))

covered <- philly_tracts %>%
  st_intersection(station_zone) %>%
  mutate(covered_area = as.numeric(st_area(.))) %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  select(GEOID, covered_area)

philly_tracts <- philly_tracts %>%
  left_join(covered, by = "GEOID") %>%
  mutate(pct_covered = replace_na(covered_area / tract_area, 0) * 100)

Notice: that last step is the left_join() from Part 1b. It’s a join by what (GEOID), used to bring a join-by-where result back into the table. The two kinds of join work together.

Part 6: The Challenge
You now have three different definitions of “has access”:

Distance: the tract centroid is within X miles of a station (dist_mi)
Touch: the tract touches the half-mile zone at all (st_filter)
Coverage: at least Y% of the tract’s area is inside the zone (pct_covered)


Your team’s task

Define “low-income.” For example, you could use the bottom quartile of tract median income, or a dollar threshold. Pick one and write it down.
Define “access.” Choose one of the three definitions above and set its threshold.
Answer the question. Which low-income tracts lack access? Produce:

The count of low-income tracts without access
A map showing them (a geom_sf() layer plus the stations)
The reliability breakdown: of those tracts, how many have High / Moderate / Low reliability income estimates?

Defend one decision in 2–3 sentences. Why this access definition and not another? How would your count change if you used a different one?

This is not a competition. There’s no leaderboard and no target RMSE. The goal is to practice the full prediction workflow on a question you choose, and to find out what actually helps. Some features you’re sure will help won’t, and some you add on a whim will. Both are findings.
You’ll:

Choose a tract-level outcome for Philadelphia and check whether it’s reliable enough to model (Weeks 2–3).
Fit a baseline model and cross-validate it (Week 5).
Pull data from Philadelphia’s open data portal through its API and build spatial features: counts, densities, and distances (Week 4, plus one new tool).
Transform variables with logs, squared terms, and categories. Watch the October 9 recorded lecture before Part 5.
Keep a model log the whole way through, and compare where your first and final models go wrong.

Timing. Parts 1–4 use only what we’ve covered through Week 5. You can finish them before the October 9 lecture. Part 5 is new material; the lecture explains it, and the instructions below give you the essentials.
Type the code yourself. The worked examples show the pattern. Your job is to apply it to your outcome and your data choices.








Important1. Don’t drop rows



Every model is cross-validated on the same tracts with the same folds, so the rows in your model log are comparable. If a new variable has missing values, fill them (for example, 0 for a count, or the median with a note) or choose a different variable. The cv_rmse() helper below will stop and tell you if you break this rule.


Your outcome comes from the 2019–2023 ACS. Pull open data from 2023 or earlier (2021–2023 is ideal). Using 2025 data to predict a 2023 outcome uses information from the future, which a real prediction model would never have.



Don’t use any variable that’s built from your outcome or measures the same thing another way. Ask yourself: would an agency trying to predict this outcome for a tract have this variable? If the answer is “only because it’s basically the outcome,” leave it out.

Sys.getenv("CENSUS_API_KEY") != ""   # should print TRUE


[1] TRUE



The cross-validation helper
This function runs 10-fold cross-validation with the same seed every time, so every model in your log is tested on the same folds. You don’t need to change it. Read it once so you know what it does.


Code
ctrl <- trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10)

cv_rmse <- function(formula, data) {
  df <- if (inherits(data, "sf")) st_drop_geometry(data) else data
  vars <- all.vars(formula)
  bad <- vars[sapply(vars, function(v) any(is.na(df[[v]])))]
  if (length(bad) > 0) {
    stop("These variables have NAs: ", paste(bad, collapse = ", "),
         ". Fill them or choose another variable (Rule 1: don't drop rows).")
  }
  set.seed(5080)
  fit <- train(formula, data = df, method = "lm", trControl = ctrl)
  fit$results$RMSE
}




The model log
Every time you fit a new model, add a row. By the end, this table is the story of your assignment.


Code
model_log <- tibble(
  model   = character(),
  added   = character(),
  cv_rmse = numeric(),
  notes   = character()
)

section: Part 3: Getting data from Philadelphia’s open data portal
text:
Part 3: Getting data from Philadelphia’s open data portal
Many of the city’s datasets on OpenDataPhilly are served through a Carto SQL API. You send a SQL query in a URL, and it sends back data. Ask for format=GeoJSON and st_read() reads the result directly, just like the Indego feed in Week 4.
The pattern:
https://phl.carto.com/api/v2/sql?format=GeoJSON&q=SELECT ... FROM table_name WHERE ...
Three pieces of SQL are all you need:

SELECT the_geom, column1, column2 chooses which columns come back. Always include the_geom, or you get no geometry.
FROM table_name chooses the dataset.
WHERE ... filters rows. Filter in the query, not in R. Some tables have millions of rows, and pulling everything will be slow or fail.

This helper builds the URL for you. Spaces and symbols in a URL need encoding, and URLencode() handles that.


Code
carto_get <- function(sql) {
  url <- paste0("https://phl.carto.com/api/v2/sql?format=GeoJSON&q=", URLencode(sql))
  st_read(url, quiet = TRUE)
}




Code
# Layer 1: Property assessments
layer1 <- carto_get(
  "SELECT the_geom, market_value, zoning
   FROM opa_properties_public
   WHERE market_value > 0
     AND market_value IS NOT NULL"
) %>%
  st_transform(st_crs(tracts))

# Layer 2: Real estate transfers
layer2 <- carto_get(
  "SELECT the_geom, document_date, total_consideration
   FROM rtt_summary
   WHERE document_date >= '2023-01-01'
     AND document_date < '2024-01-01'
     AND total_consideration > 0
     AND document_type = 'DEED'"
) %>%
  st_transform(st_crs(tracts))








Note



Answer: Why these layers? What do you expect them to capture that the ACS variables don’t?
Because of the obvious disparity in residual values in high and low-income areas of the city, I decided to examine the real estate transfers in different areas of the city to help identify “desirable” areas with higher property values and more active housing markets. I want to see if desirable areas match exactly with the high residual values in my initial map.
I also want to examine the distribution of the white population because a glance at the white population map shows a near-exact overlap with my map of high residual values. This isn’t meant to imply that race itself causes the difference in income, but it helps explore my analysis on how immigrant populations tend to be much poorer and less stable than the settled-in white population.

title: Assignment: Building Features, Watching What Happens
text:
Part 7: Reflection
In my model, the feature that improved predicted performance the most was the percentage of non-Hispanic white residents in a census tract; this reduced the CV RMSE from approximately $30,303 to $21,207, a substantial improvement. However, my second feature, the real estate transfer density, did not significantly improve my model. In some ways, this makes sense — families living in expensive suburban homes are likely to have a stable source of income that gives them both the means and an incentive to remain in one place. On the other hand, young professionals in the city core making high salaries may be more transient; thus, the real estate transfer density cannot predict either low or high income accurately.
My strongest coefficient, pct_white, is 803.986. Its β̂ reading predicts about an $804 higher median household income for each 1-percent increase in non-Hispanic white population, if all other variables remain constant. Its ŷ reading is that, for 2 otherwise similar census tracts whose white population shares differ by 10 percentage points, the model predicts median household income to differ by approximately $8040.
However, there are still significant areas of error in my map. The model continues to undershoot the median income values of the wealthiest neighborhoods in Philadelphia. This suggests that my current predictors do not fully capture all the factors driving high incomes in these areas. I believe that adding another factor (percentage of those with a bachelor’s degree or higher) will explain the variance much better.
Finally, there doesn’t seem to be a strong visible trend between the CV of my outcome estimate and the absolute size of the residual. This suggests that tracts with greater relative uncertainty in their ACS income estimates do not necessarily have larger model prediction errors. However, it is difficult to tell how much remaining error is simply statistical noise. Some error may come from variations in ACS sampling, while others may come from genuine differences between the neighborhoods.

If we have some data on where rents exceed our expectation, and we want to predict where rents will exceed a specific threshold:

Income = 30,000 -> rent = 1000
Income = 100,000 -> rent = 3000
Income = 250,000 -> rent = 6000

We can have a formula:
\(Y = f(x) + e\)
Where Y is rent, f(x) is unknown, and e is everything else.
We can use different kinds of classifiers, from linear (rigid but easy to explain/interpret) to neural networks (flexible but complex).
The linear regression equation comes up with a best-fit line:

Cross-Validation
K-Fold -> we split the data into several chunks, called folds.

Shuffle the data and split it into k distinct groups
For each iteration, use one group as the test set and the remaining k-1 groups combined as their training set
Repeat for each fold, and evaluate the RMSE for each one; lower RMSE is better

“My spatial stats class says use a spatial lag model”
[y = W y + X+ ]
That’s the right tool for inference about spillovers. For prediction it fails three ways:

It needs neighbors’ prices. To price a house, you’d need the prices of houses that haven’t sold yet.
It leaks. In CV, a test house’s neighbors in the training set carry its answer.
It explains nothing. “Near expensive houses” is not a reason a policymaker can act on.

Our rule: spatial features of X, never Y. Crime near the house is fine; prices near the house are not.

check_na <- function(formula, df) {
  vars <- all.vars(formula)
  bad <- vars[sapply(vars, function(v) any(is.na(df[[v]])))]
  if (length(bad) > 0) {
    stop("These variables have NAs: ", paste(bad, collapse = ", "),
         ". Fill them or choose another variable (Rule 1).")
  }
}

# 10-fold CV RMSE, same folds every time
cv_rmse <- function(formula, data) {
  df <- if (inherits(data, "sf")) st_drop_geometry(data) else data
  check_na(formula, df)
  set.seed(5080)
  fit <- train(formula, data = df, method = "lm",
               trControl = trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10))
  fit$results$RMSE
}

# Each house's prediction from the fold where it was held out
cv_pred <- function(formula, data) {
  df <- if (inherits(data, "sf")) st_drop_geometry(data) else data
  check_na(formula, df)
  set.seed(5080)
  fit <- train(formula, data = df, method = "lm",
               trControl = trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10,
                                        savePredictions = "final"))
  fit$pred %>% arrange(rowIndex) %>% pull(pred)
}

# Chicago Data Portal (Socrata) -> sf. `where` is a SoQL filter.
socrata_get <- function(dataset, where, select = NULL, limit = 200000) {
  where <- str_squish(where)
  q <- paste0("$where=", URLencode(where, reserved = TRUE), "&$limit=", limit)
  if (!is.null(select)) q <- paste0(q, "&$select=", URLencode(str_squish(select), reserved = TRUE))
  url <- paste0("https://data.cityofchicago.org/resource/", dataset, ".geojson?", q)
  tmp <- tempfile(fileext = ".geojson")
  resp <- tryCatch(download.file(url, tmp, quiet = TRUE), error = function(e) e)
  if (inherits(resp, "error")) stop("Portal request failed. Open this URL in a browser to see why:\n", url)
  st_read(tmp, quiet = TRUE)
}

Function for Moran’s \(I\) of the residuals. NOTE: Distance bands were used to handle instances of identical points (such as condos in the same building)


Code
moran_resid <- function(formula, data, k = 8) {
  mod <- lm(formula, data = data)
  
  # Spatial weights matrix 
  coords <- st_coordinates(st_centroid(st_geometry(data)))
  nb <- dnearneigh(coords, d1 = 0, d2 = 500)      
  lw <- nb2listw(nb, style = "W", zero.policy = TRUE)
  moran.test(residuals(mod), lw, zero.policy = TRUE)
  
  # Moran's I of residuals 
  mt <- moran.test(residuals(mod), lw)
  unname(mt$estimate["Moran I statistic"])
}

4A. Where does your final model fail worst? Is it guessing too high or too low there, and why do you think so?
4B. Assessors judge their work with the ratio of predicted value to sale price. A ratio above 1 means the home is over-valued and its owner over-taxed. Does your model’s ratio differ by neighborhood income? Connect your answer to your Part 1 cleaning rules and to “The Tax Divide.”

               geometry = TRUE) |>
  st_transform(3435)

  mutate(income_quintile = ntile(estimate, 5)) |>
  group_by(income_quintile) |>
  summarise(median_ratio = median(ratio, na.rm = TRUE), n = n())


Your answers:
4A: The final model under-predicted the most in the northeastern side on the city where houses sold for $500,000 or more above the prediction. On a smaller scale, there are streaks of over-predictions within this area too where houses sold under the prediction by a margin of $500,000 or more. These failures could be due to the high variation between block prices within this community that is not factored within the model.
4B: With the calculated ratios between the predicted values and the actual sale prices of the houses, this was added with income data from the Census to determine if the “Tax Divide” describes in the Tribune is seen in our model. Based on the table above, the ratios for all 5 quintiles hovers around 1, with the lowest income quintile (1) being just above 1. There is a slight dip below 1 in the median ratio for income quintiles 2, 3, and 4, before approaching 1 in the highest income quintile (5). Thus, our model’s median ratio does not differ by income.

The r-squared of the final model is approximately 0.773, meaning it explains 77.3 percent of the variation in sale prices in the training data. The remaining 22.7 percent of the variation is due to unidentified characteristics (which may include factors such as crime rate or proximity to factories). With additional time, this model could be improved on with the identification of additional predictors.
Although adding additional predictors and neighborhood effects decreased our RMSE approximately 22.8 percent, our final RMSE ($226,544) suggests that there is still a substantial amount of prediction errors in the model. The final model’s Moran’s I of approximately 0.240 suggests a weak-to-moderate clustering effect across our residuals, which could potentially indicate that nearby properties could share characteristics that the model did not fully capture. To be confident in this model’s predictive power, we would need to examine additional neighborhood-level characteristics and reevaluate the model to reduce the uneven predictive accuracy across Chicago.
Overall, we suggest that this model is useful as a preliminary, exploratory tool to get a sense of house values, but it should not be relied on alone to determine assessed values. It should certainly not be considered an end-all assessment of house values.
